text: Hello and thank you very much for joining my short presentation on AI and competition. My name is Jan Oster and I'm a professor of media law and the law of digitization at Osnabrück University. Last year when I attended this conference, I gave a presentation on AI and pluralism or diversity of opinion. This year I'm taking a slightly different perspective on what is more or less the same topic, namely the perspective of competition law. Social networks operate algorithmic systems that aggregate, select and present content, thereby influencing opinion formation. And AI generated content such as Google Gemini or ChatGPT is increasingly serving as a source of information. So rather than to Google a certain information, people increasingly ask ChatGPT and then they get just one single answer for their question.

summary: This is a problem for media law, this is a problem for media regulation, something I addressed last year, but it's also a problem for competition law, right.
text: This is a problem for media law, this is a problem for media regulation, something I addressed last year, but it's also a problem for competition law, right. Rather than different provider, service providers offering their services as competitors, people increasingly tend to use one service provider to get certain information. And this I think raises certain challenges that we have to address. When it comes to AI and competition, two problems need to be addressed. One is the threat to competition posed by AI, meaning threats to competition via the application of a certain AI system. Second, the opportunities, but also the threats to competition for AI, meaning the development level, the development of AI systems. Let me briefly begin with the first pillar, AI poses a threat to competition.

Using Generative AI is like having a magic wand. Instead of giving the user superpowers, the real trick in using Generative AI is making people believe they have superpowers, simply because they have used it. text: My name is Jess Rose Smith, and I'm a Technology Policy Manager in Off-Com's online safety group. And today I'm going to give an overview of harmful deepfakes and what they mean for online safety. Off-Com is the UK's independent communications regulator, and we oversee several sectors across telecoms, broadcast TV and radio, online video sharing and post. Off-Com recently became the new regulator for online safety. The UK's Online Safety Act 2023 is a new set of laws that protect children and adults online. They play safety duties on social media companies and search services. And these duties include taking down illegal content and preventing children from accessing harmful content. Off-Com has published draft codes of practice which set out how services can comply with the act.

summary: And we also have a broad range of powers to enforce compliance.
text: And we also have a broad range of powers to enforce compliance. But why we're interested in deepfakes? Public concern about deepfakes has increased substantially in recent months. These fears have been stoked by several high profile incidents such as the deep fake images of Taylor Swift that weren't viral on mainstream social media platforms and a fake audio that purportedly depicted London Mayor as the deep-can't criticising last year's Amasith Day Parades. While these and other well-known cases feature public figures and major institutions, deepfakes are also doing serious harm to ordinary individuals, whether that's being featured in non-consensual sexual deepfake videos or falling victim to deepfake fraudulent adverts. As the new regulator for online safety, Off-Com is committed to doing its part to curtail the circulation of these harmful deepfakes.

summary: But to do that, we've needed to have a clear understanding of the type of deepfakes that can be created, the harms they're most likely to be implicated in, their prevalence and the merits and limitations...
text: But to do that, we've needed to have a clear understanding of the type of deepfakes that can be created, the harms they're most likely to be implicated in, their prevalence and the merits and limitations of different mitigation techniques. So what are deepfakes? Deepfakes can take many forms of encompassing audio, video and image content, often they involve showing a real person doing or saying something that they're not. However, they can also depict entirely fictional characters and may be absent of people altogether, so they might present staged events such as a fake image of a battlefield in a war zone. While some deepfakes consist of wholly new novel content, others take the form of existing content that has been manipulated, so where a real video has been edited to manipulate a person's mouth movements and dubbed audio has been added in.

summary: We identify three main ways that deepfakes can cause harm, those that demean, defraud and disinform.
text: We identify three main ways that deepfakes can cause harm, those that demean, defraud and disinform. Deepfakes that demean are created to humiliate or abuse a victim survivor by falsely depicting them in a certain manner or performing a certain act, for example, in sexual activity. The impact of these deepfakes is often devastating. In the intention of the perpetrator, maybe to abuse or bully a victim survivor to extort money or force the victim survivor to share further content. Deepfakes that defraud are used to deceive a target by misrepresenting someone else's identity. They are primarily used to assist fraudulent behaviour such as scam communications and false advertising. And the target of defrauding deepfakes isn't necessarily important and they can be channeled multiple individuals simultaneously.

summary: Deepfakes that disinform are used to sow distrust or spread disinformation across a large group.
text: Deepfakes that disinform are used to sow distrust or spread disinformation across a large group. Their objectives often are to influence or shape societal opinion on key political or social issues such as elections, war, religion or health. However, not all content created by technology is harmful. Synthetic content has many positive benefits and in online safety we're seeing it being used to plug gaps in training data sets that are required to build really important forms of safety technology. Synthetic content could also be satirical or comedic. And in our desire to address harmful deepfakes we really need to be mindful not to undermine the creation of legitimate or innocuous content. Deepfakes do appear to have become more prevalent over time.

summary: Ofcom's recent poll on deepfakes found that 43% of adult respondents and 50% of child respondents believe that they had encountered a deepfake at least once in the last six months.
text: Ofcom's recent poll on deepfakes found that 43% of adult respondents and 50% of child respondents believe that they had encountered a deepfake at least once in the last six months. And based on the available evidence it appears that the most common form of deepfake shared online is non-consensual intimate content. Leading campaign group my image my choice estimate that there are now over 276,000 videos of this nature circulating on the most popular deepfake sites was over 4.2 billion total views. The overwhelming majority of this content is thought to feature women. We found though that more broadly it can be challenging to accurately quantify the scale in reach of deepfakes. This is because definitions of what constitutes a deepfake can vary and since deepfakes are designed to be deceptive many will go undocumented.

summary: We found that some major online platforms disclose information on things like the number of fake accounts or the amount of nude or synthetic content that has been identified but non-published metrics specifically on deepfake content.
text: We found that some major online platforms disclose information on things like the number of fake accounts or the amount of nude or synthetic content that has been identified but non-published metrics specifically on deepfake content. As such we've relied on public surveys, third party research as well as our own to understand prevalence although this often indicates volume rather than the number of user impressions. So why are the number of deepfakes increasing? The first deepfakes were created using two forms of AI that have existed for many years. However, the use of these technologies have been overtaken by the availability of new tools which are powered by generative AI and allow users to create wholly novel content that is significantly more convincing and lifelike.

summary: These tools have also made it easier to create deepfakes so that anyone with really modest technical skills can do so many generative AI tools also available free of charge.
text: These tools have also made it easier to create deepfakes so that anyone with really modest technical skills can do so many generative AI tools also available free of charge. Another important driver behind the increase in deepfakes online is the grace of what we have called the deepfakes economy. This consists of a number of elements. Firstly, individual creators offering to create deepfakes for very small sums of money. Secondly, the launch of user-friendly apps that serves to make generative AI models even more accessible and can include standalone chat box and so-called notification apps.

summary: Added to this is the proliferation of websites that are dedicated to hosted deepfake content and which share manuals that explain how to create such content.

These can also be easily accessed through search engines. So what can be done to address deepfakes? Addressing them is likely to require action from all actors in the supply chain. From the developers that create generative AI models and related tools to the platforms that host this technology and user-facing services that act as spaces for deepfake content to be shared and amplified. In our research, we identified four main routes for actors to mitigate deepfakes. Prevention involves efforts to limit the creation of harmful deepfakes and this can include adopting filters to prevent models being able to create certain types of content like nude content.

summary: Embedding involves attaching contextual information to synthetic media through tools like watermarks and labels.
text: Embedding involves attaching contextual information to synthetic media through tools like watermarks and labels. Many organizations have started to sign up to various content provenance and authenticity schemes. Detection encompasses efforts to distinguish real from fake content. One means of detecting deepfakes is by using machine learning classifiers that have been trained on known deepfake content. And finally enforcement involves setting clear rules about the types of synthetic content that are allowed to be created and shared on online services. It also requires acting against users that breach these rules for example through suspending or removing user accounts. All of the above interventions show promise and helping to mitigate the creation and spread of harmful deepfakes. But it's important to acknowledge their limitations and weak spots.

summary: Prevention measures like prompt filters for example need to be used carefully to avoid blocking the creation of legitimate content like political satire.

Instead, we look more broadly at the concept that we term the human or machine issue, the H or M issue. In a future world, when in some interactions, machines will be able to mimic humans impressively, new social, psychological, functional and obviously technical issues are bound to become relevant. So here are some of the questions that come to mind immediately and in this paper, we actually discuss them.
